failure_modes: Spike-in non‑representativeness: spike‑in EVs differ in surface composition, size, rigidity, or cargo protection and therefore survive formulation/device stresses that destroy or mask endogenous EVs, producing false-positive pass results.

Undetected assay interference: capture reagents or buffers could generate artifactual recovery of protein/particle signal (e.g., detergent‑insensitive aggregates, reagent precipitates) that mimic spike-in readouts despite capture‑compatibility controls being imperfect.

Bioassay disconnect: the in vitro membrane‑protected anti‑inflammatory assay may not predict relevant in vivo potency or route‑specific efficacy (intranasal-to-brain exposure), so passing the gate may not translate to therapeutic effect.

Species/route translation failure: even with preserved orthogonal identity and in vitro activity, intranasal delivery in large animals or humans may still yield negligible brain exposure due to species‑specific clearance or nasal retention, confounding bridging decisions.

Insufficient sensitivity or dynamic range: endogenous signals may be below detection limits post‑exposure while spike‑in is detectable, making co‑localization and detergent/protease sensitivity appear preserved when endogenous material is absent.

Lot heterogeneity: high lot‑to‑lot variability in conditioned‑medium product could produce inconsistent endogenous readouts that are masked by consistent spike‑in behavior, undermining reproducibility criteria.

Detergent/protease artifacts: membrane disruption controls (detergent+protease) could incompletely distinguish true membrane protection from tightly bound non‑vesicular complexes, leading to misclassification.

Capture‑reagent buffer incompatibility: capture antibodies/affinity reagents may have unrecognized sensitivity to excipients or device rinse matrices, producing variable recovery that is not fully corrected by the proposed compatibility controls.
strongest_objection: The single strongest bounded failure mode is that the exogenous intact‑EV spike‑in will not faithfully mimic the physicochemical and capture/functional behavior of the endogenous clinical‑source EV population after formulation and device passage; as a result, spike‑in preservation could produce a false‑positive compatibility signal (spike-in preserved while endogenous EV identity or membrane‑protected bioactivity are lost or altered), leading to advancement of lots that are not biologically equivalent or effective in vivo.
